item.title: cms — signatures in CMS SignedData
item.description:
Does this signature hold over these bytes, and which certificate made it? CMS SignedData (RFC 5652) is the container a PDF signature, a UEFI authenticated variable and an S/MIME message are written in. The standard library reads certificates and checks signatures,but has no CMS.

go get github.com/go-authn/cms@v0.2.1

Since v0.2.1, Verify refuses an attribute-less signature whose signed content is itself a DER SET OF Attribute carrying both a content-type and a message-digest attribute. A signature made with signed attributes covers their DER (RFC 5652§5.4); re-packed without the key as a SignedData without signed attributes, whose content is those attributes, it verified and named the signer for content never signed as content.

v0.2.0 reads, verifies and signs.

Example 

package main

import (
 "crypto/x509"
 "errors"
 "fmt"
 "os"

 "github.com/go-authn/cms"
)

func main() {
 // A detached signature and the bytes it signed. For a PDF these are the
 // signature dictionary's /Contents and the file's /ByteRange.
 der, err := os.ReadFile("signature.der")
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 content, err := os.ReadFile("signed-bytes")
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }

 sd, err := cms.Parse(der)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 signers, err := sd.Verify(content) // nil instead, when the content is attached
 switch {
 case errors.Is(err, cms.ErrInvalid):
 fmt.Println("the signature does not hold:", err)
 return
 case errors.Is(err, cms.ErrUnsupported):
 fmt.Println("a signature this package cannot check:", err)
 return
 case err != nil: // cms.ErrMalformed
 fmt.Println("not a signature:", err)
 return
 }

 // The signature holds. Whether to TRUST who made it is a second question,
 // with inputs of its own: the roots you accept.
 roots := x509.NewCertPool() // fill with the roots you trust
 for _, c := range signers {
 _, err := c.Verify(x509.VerifyOptions{Roots: roots, KeyUsages: []x509.ExtKeyUsage{x509.ExtKeyUsageAny}})
 fmt.Println(c.Subject, "chain:", err)
 }
}

Verify answers whether the signature holds. Trust — the certificate’s chain, its validity, its revocation — is a separate decision, which RFC 5652§5.6 places outside CMS: crypto/x509 for the chain, andgo-authn/revocation’s CRL verification for what has been taken back.

Signing

cms.Sign writes one DER ContentInfo with one signer, from anycrypto.Signer: an RSA, ECDSA or Ed25519 key, held in a file, on a card or in an HSM. Before it returns, it verifies the signature under the certificate, so a signer that hands back a wrong signature is refused, never emitted.

package main

import (
 "crypto"
 "crypto/ecdsa"
 "crypto/elliptic"
 "crypto/rand"
 "crypto/x509"
 "crypto/x509/pkix"
 "errors"
 "fmt"
 "math/big"
 "time"

 "github.com/go-authn/cms"
)

func main() {
 // A key and a self-signed certificate, for the example. In practice the
 // key may live on a card or in an HSM: any crypto.Signer will do.
 key, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 template := &x509.Certificate{
 SerialNumber: big.NewInt(1),
 Subject: pkix.Name{CommonName: "signer"},
 NotBefore: time.Now().Add(-time.Hour),
 NotAfter: time.Now().Add(time.Hour),
 KeyUsage: x509.KeyUsageDigitalSignature,
 }
 certDER, err := x509.CreateCertificate(rand.Reader, template, template, key.Public(), key)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 cert, err := x509.ParseCertificate(certDER)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }

 content := []byte("the bytes to sign")
 der, err := cms.Sign(content, cms.SignOptions{
 Signer: key,
 Certificate: cert,
 Hash: crypto.SHA256,
 Detached: true, // as a PDF signature: the content is not inside
 SigningTime: time.Now(),
 })
 switch {
 case errors.Is(err, cms.ErrSigner):
 panic(fmt.Sprint("the key or the device failed: ", err))
 case errors.Is(err, cms.ErrOptions):
 panic(fmt.Sprint("the request is wrong: ", err))
 case err != nil: // cms.ErrUnsupported
 panic(err)
 }

 // Sign checked its own signature; Verify is the reader's side.
 sd, err := cms.Parse(der)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 signers, err := sd.Verify(content)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 fmt.Println("signed by", signers[0].Subject.CommonName)

 content[0] ^= 1
 _, err = sd.Verify(content)
 fmt.Println("altered content:", errors.Is(err, cms.ErrInvalid))
}

SignOptions also takes Chain (intermediates to embed), PSS (RSASSA-PSS),SigningCertificateV2 (RFC 5035, what CAdES and PAdES baseline require),ContentType, NoSignedAttrs and Rand. The digest is SHA-256 by default, or SHA-384 or SHA-512; Ed25519 always uses SHA-512. SHA-1 is refused.

Sign has three errors of its own: ErrOptions (the request is wrong),ErrSigner (the key or device failed, or returned a signature that does not verify under the certificate) and ErrUnsupported (an algorithm it does not write). Ed25519 without signed attributes is refused too: RFC 8419 allows it, but OpenSSL does not verify what this package would write.

OpenSSL’s cms -verify and this package’s Verify agree on every combination it was asked about: 58 combinations, 203 verdicts, over RSA PKCS #1 v1.5,RSA-PSS and ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, and Ed25519 with SHA-512, attached and detached, with and without signed attributes. Verify does not yet check signing-certificate-v2: pinning the signer’s certificate to that attribute is the caller’s.

Three errors, because a caller needs three answers

error means
ErrMalformed not a SignedData this package can read
ErrUnsupported a signature, using something not implemented here
ErrInvalid readable and supported, and the signature does not hold

Every refusal wraps exactly one of them, and the fuzz tests hold that as an invariant.

What it refuses

From the code, each with a test that asserts its message:

  • a signer whose certificate is not in the container;
  • signed attributes without exactly one content-type and exactly onemessage-digest, each with a single value;
  • a signed content type that is not the content’s;
  • a digest that does not match the content — recomputed here, never taken from the signer;
  • a signature algorithm whose own hash is not the digest’s;
  • SHA-1, refused by name;
  • Ed25519 over anything but SHA-512 (RFC 8419);
  • signed attributes in four non-DER shapes: a primitive [0] tag (one bit away from a valid signature), an attribute that is not a SEQUENCE, values that are not a SET, and bytes trailing inside an attribute. The order of the SET is not checked;
  • more than 16 signers, and more than 16 MiB. A size bound is not a work bound, which is why the signers are capped: the content is hashed once per digest algorithm, but an Ed25519 signer without signed attributes still hashes all of it on every check.

Not yet: BER indefinite lengths are refused rather than guessed at;signing is one signer, with no counter-signatures and no timestamp token;Verify does not check signing-certificate-v2; no chain validation, on purpose.

What it is checked against

OpenSSL’s cms command. Eleven signatures made by OpenSSL 4.1.0 cover RSA,RSA-PSS, ECDSA and Ed25519, with attached and detached content and both signer-identifier forms. openssl cms -verify and this package give the same verdict on every one and on its tampered variants: 34 of 34.

On two points the package is stricter than OpenSSL 4.1.0, which accepts a primitive signed-attributes tag and Ed25519 over SHA-256.

item.title: pkcs12 — the key and certificates inside a .p12 upload
item.description:
What private key and certificates are inside this file somebody sent us? PKCS#12 (RFC 7292) is the .p12 /.pfx container an exporter writes a key, its certificate and the rest of the chain into. golang.org/x/crypto/pkcs12 is deprecated and frozen on SHA-1 and 3DES/RC2, so it rejects what OpenSSL 3 and 4 and current Windows write by default (PBES2, AES, SHA-2 MACs). This module reads those, with no dependency beyond the standard library, and is built for untrusted uploads.

go get github.com/go-authn/pkcs12@v0.1.1

It decodes only: there is no encoder. Whether to trust the chain iscrypto/x509’s Verify, a separate decision.

Example 

package main

import (
 "errors"
 "fmt"
 "os"

 "github.com/go-authn/pkcs12"
)

func main() {
 data, err := os.ReadFile("upload.p12")
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }

 b, err := pkcs12.Decode(data, "the password", nil)
 switch {
 case errors.Is(err, pkcs12.ErrIncorrectPassword):
 fmt.Println("ask again:", err)
 return
 case err != nil: // hostile, unsupported, too costly...
 fmt.Println("refused:", err)
 return
 }

 // b.PrivateKey *rsa.PrivateKey, *ecdsa.PrivateKey, ed25519.PrivateKey or *ecdh.PrivateKey
 // b.Certificate the certificate holding the key's public half
 // b.CACerts every other certificate, in file order
 fmt.Println("certificate for", b.Certificate.Subject, "and", len(b.CACerts), "more")
}

Decode(data, password, *Options) (*Bundle, error) takes nil for the defaults. The Bundle holds the key, the certificate whose public half it is,and the others in file order.

Options and their defaults

A zero field means the default, and no field can switch a bound off.

field default meaning
MaxInputSize 8 MiB len(data)
MaxIterations 1 000 000 iterations of any one key derivation
MaxWork 5 000 000 iterations x output blocks over the whole file
MaxDepth 16 BER nesting and constructed-string chunk nesting
MaxBags 1024 SafeBags in the file
MaxAuthSafes 32 ContentInfos in the AuthenticatedSafe
MaxCertSize 32 KiB DER of one certificate
MaxCertBytes 512 KiB DER of all certificates together
MaxRSABits 8192 RSA modulus
AllowNoMAC false read a file with no integrity MAC (openssl pkcs12 -nomac); otherwise it is ErrNoMAC
NoPassword false the file was exported with no password at all, as opposed to the empty password ""

The two booleans are the format’s two ambiguities. With AllowNoMAC, nothing authenticates the content, and a wrong password is only noticed by a failed decryption. The empty password ("") and the absent password(NoPassword) derive different keys and both work: with "" and NoPassword false, Decode tries the empty one first and then the absent one, because exporters disagree about which they wrote; with NoPassword true only the absent one is tried, and the password argument must be "".

What it reads

layer supported
encryption PBES2 (RFC 8018) with PBKDF2 over HMAC-SHA-1/224/256/384/512 and AES-128/192/256-CBC
legacy encryption pbeWithSHAAnd3-KeyTripleDES-CBC, pbeWithSHAAnd2-KeyTripleDES-CBC, pbeWithSHAAnd40BitRC2-CBC and the 128-bit variant; RC2 is implemented in the module
integrity HMAC MAC with SHA-1/224/256/384/512 (RFC 7292 Appendix B KDF), and PBMAC1 (RFC 9579)
passwords BMPString per Appendix B.1, non-BMP characters as surrogate pairs
encoding BER, including indefinite lengths and constructed OCTET STRINGs, which Windows and Java write
bags shrouded and plain key bags, certificate bags; CRL, secret and safe-contents bags are skipped

Refused as ErrUnsupported: public-key integrity and privacy modes(signedData, envelopedData), RC4, scrypt, PBES1 other than the PKCS#12 ones, SHA-1 inside PBMAC1, and BER (rather than DER) inside a certificate or a PKCS#8 key.

Errors

error means
ErrMalformed not a PKCS#12 file this package can read
ErrUnsupported readable, using something not implemented here
ErrLimit a bound of Options would be exceeded; refused before the work
ErrIncorrectPassword a wrong password and a tampered file, the same answer by design
ErrNoMAC no MAC, and AllowNoMAC is not set
ErrNoPrivateKey no private key in the file
ErrMultipleKeys more than one private key in the file
ErrNoCertificate no certificate matches the private key
ErrPassword a password that cannot be used

Every refusal wraps exactly one of them, and the fuzz target holds that as an invariant.

The security bounds

Every bound above is checked before the work, and every length field is checked against the bytes actually present before anything is allocated. Salts over 512 bytes and passwords over 1024 characters are refused.

The MAC is verified, in constant time, before anything is decrypted.

crypto/x509 allocates up to 43 to 52 times a certificate’s size when it is made of thousands of tiny names, and crypto/rsa validates a key by arithmetic on the numbers it declares, so factors far longer than the modulus cost superlinear CPU. Neither can be fixed from outside, so what reaches them is bounded first: certificates by MaxCertSize and MaxCertBytes, and every PKCS#8 key (32 KiB at most) is read with encoding/asn1 and refused, typed,when its modulus exceeds MaxRSABits, a factor or exponent is longer than the modulus allows, a number is not positive, or it is multi-prime(ErrUnsupported).

Memory per request. With the default options, a hostile file makes oneDecode allocate about 25 MB (measured jointly: worst certificates and the largest accepted key, 8192 bits, 25.1 MB, of which about 20 MB stay live until it returns) for a file of 530 KB. A service decoding uploads should cap the decodes in flight, for instance with a semaphore, and lower MaxCertBytes if it expects only short chains.

Limitations

  • RSA keys without CRT values are refused (ErrUnsupported). A key lackingDp, Dq and Qinv is refused before crypto/x509 sees it. RFC 8017 requires them and every exporter writes them (OpenSSL, Windows, Java keytool), but crypto/x509 derives missing ones with big-number arithmetic:16.4 MB and 21 744 allocations at 8192 bits, against 0.36 MB and 618 with them.
  • RSA CRT values are verified, whatever GODEBUG says (go-authn/pkcs12#2, fixed in v0.1.1). Before crypto/x509 sees the key, Dp = D mod (P-1),Dq = D mod (Q-1) and Qinv × Q = 1 mod P are checked, after the size bounds; a mismatch is refused as ErrMalformed. UnderGODEBUG=x509rsacrt=0 the standard library drops wrong CRT values and computes them again, which took a decode with the worst certificates to 39.4 MB (ratio 74.7), outside the bound the tests assert. The check does not depend on the setting.
  • It decodes only, and does not judge the chain.

What it is checked against

OpenSSL is the judge. 23 files written by OpenSSL 4.1 (AES/PBES2,-legacy 3DES and RC2, -nomac, several certificates, RSA, EC and Ed25519,PBMAC1) are in the tests, with a manifest of what OpenSSL itself says each holds.

Amplification. TestAmplification bounds allocated bytes over input bytes on many tiny bags, many certificates, deep indefinite nesting, long OCTET STRING chains and 4 GiB length claims, and asserts that the refusals happen before crypto/x509 is called. The module is also fuzzed (corpus committed),holds 100 % block coverage and is run with -race and govulncheck.

software.sslmate.com/src/go-pkcs12, in a separate oracle/ module: on the 23 files both can attempt, both read 18 with byte-identical leaf, chain order and key. Only this package reads the other 5 (RC2-128, a SHA-384 MAC, no MAC, and two passwords with characters outside the BMP); there is none the other reads and this one refuses.

It pairs with cms: decode a .p12 here,sign there.

item.title: servercert — where a daemon's TLS certificate comes from
item.description:
Where does a daemon’s TLS server certificate come from? A certificate and key on disk, re-read when they change, or an ACME CA throughautocert, External Account Binding included.

go get github.com/go-authn/servercert@v0.7.0

A Config names exactly one source — CertFile and KeyFile, or ACME —and New returns a *Source whose TLSConfig() serves it, withMinVersion TLS 1.2.

Example

From files:

package main

import (
 "log"
 "net/http"

 "github.com/go-authn/servercert"
)

func main() {
 src, err := servercert.New(servercert.Config{
 CertFile: "/etc/fileshare/tls/fullchain.pem",
 KeyFile: "/etc/fileshare/tls/privkey.pem",
 OnError: func(err error) { log.Print(err) }, // a renewal that did not load
 })
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err) // unreadable, unparsable, or a key that is not the certificate's
 }
 srv := &http.Server{Addr: ":443", TLSConfig: src.TLSConfig()}
 log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServeTLS("", ""))
}

Config.Check refuses a configuration that cannot work, and touches nothing —no file read, no directory created:

package main

import (
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/servercert"
)

func main() {
 // Check touches nothing: no file is read, no directory created.
 for _, c := range []servercert.Config{
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"*.example.org"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme"}},
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"192.0.2.10"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme"}},
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"files.example.org"}, CacheDir: "acme"}},
 {CertFile: "/etc/fileshare/tls/fullchain.pem"},
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"files.example.org"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme",
 DirectoryURL: "http://acme.example.org/directory"}},
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"files.example.org"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme"}},
 } {
 fmt.Println(c.Check())
 }
}
servercert: ACME domain "*.example.org" is a wildcard; that needs dns-01, which autocert does not do
servercert: ACME domain "192.0.2.10" is an IP address; autocert issues only for DNS names
servercert: ACME.CacheDir "acme" is not an absolute path
servercert: CertFile and KeyFile go together; one of them is empty
servercert: ACME.DirectoryURL "http://acme.example.org/directory" is not an https URL (RFC 8555 §6.1)
<nil>

The last one is Let’s Encrypt production: DirectoryURL empty.

Files

New reads the pair and fails now on one that is unreadable, does not parse, or whose key is not the certificate’s. After that, at most once every 10 seconds and during a handshake, the files are read again; a changed pair is parsed without holding a lock and swapped in. A changed pair that does not load — the certificate written before its key, a truncated file — is reported once to OnError, and the last good pair stays in service, so a renewal job that writes the two files one after the other never takes the server down.

ACME

autocert answers two challenge types and no other: tls-alpn-01 (RFC 8737,port 443, ALPN acme-tls/1) and, with HTTPChallenge, http-01 (RFC 8555§8.3, port 80, served by Source.HTTPHandler). Without ACME.DNS there is nodns-01, hence no wildcard; an IP-address certificate is never issued.

dns-01: a server the CA cannot reach (since v0.7.0)

ACME.DNS proves control of the names with a TXT record at_acme-challenge.<name> (RFC 8555 §8.4). The server needs no inbound port and may sit on a private LAN address, and Domains may hold a wildcard(*.school.example, which does not cover school.example: list both).Issuance goes through x/crypto/acme (autocert has no dns-01): one certificate for every name, kept 0600 in CacheDir, renewed in the background, the old one serving meanwhile. DNS excludes HTTPChallenge.

DNS: &servercert.DNS{
 CredentialsFile: "/etc/relay/dns-update.conf", // 0600, owned by the user
 Provider: func(b []byte) (servercert.DNSSolver, error) { return rfc2136.New(b) },
 Resolver: "192.0.2.53:53", // optional: wait until the TXT is visible there
}

A provider is two methods, Present(ctx, name, value) andCleanUp(ctx, name, value), each on one TXT value (a wildcard and its base name share one record name). The credentials file is read under the checks ofEABHMACKeyFile and handed to Provider; never an argument, an environment variable or a URL. The module github.com/go-authn/servercert/rfc2136 (v0.1.0)is the provider for a name server that takes RFC 2136 dynamic updates signed with TSIG (RFC 8945): server, zone, key, algorithm (hmac-sha256, -384 or -512) and secret in one file.

Certificates are obtained at the first handshake whose SNI names one ofDomains, or before any client by Source.Prefetch, and renewed by autocert before they expire. A client that connects by IP address sends no SNI and is served the first domain’s certificate.

Append to NextProtos, never replace it

With ACME, TLSConfig().NextProtos holds acme-tls/1, without which the CA’s tls-alpn-01 validation fails. And append you must: a Go TLS server that advertises ALPN protocols refuses a client whose offer shares none, so an NFS-over-TLS server adds sunrpc (RFC 9289). net/http adds http/1.1 andh2 itself.

A CA that needs no challenge. autocert returns at once when a new order is already ready, which is what a CA with pre-validated domains answers: GÉANT TCS, served by HARICA, for an Enterprise Admin account. An internal server reachable on neither port 80 nor 443 from the Internet can still get a publicly trusted certificate. The EAB HMAC key is a secret, so the configuration names a file holding it (EABHMACKeyFile), never the key.

One defect of x/crypto/acme is worked around (golang/go#77704):after finalizing an order the CA is still processing, the client polls the URL in the finalize response’s Location header, which RFC 8555 does not put there. servercert gives the ACME client a transport that adds that header, with the order’s URL from the earlier newOrder response.

What it refuses, and why

Check refuses: neither or both sources; half a file pair; ACME without domains or cache directory; a relative path; half an EAB; a domain that is an IP address, a wildcard, a single label, ends with a dot, or is not a valid host name; a directory URL that is not https (RFC 8555 §6.1).

New also refuses a cache directory — it holds private keys — that is a symbolic link, is accessible by group or others, is owned by a user other than the process’s effective user, or cannot be written; a missing one is created0700 and checked after. Every directory above it must be changeable only by root or the effective user, as sshd’s StrictModes asks of the path toauthorized_keys, and a symbolic link above it is refused unless root owns it.On Windows, mode and owner are not checked — ACLs decide both, and restricting them is yours — and a symbolic link anywhere in the path is refused.

New (and every reload) also refuses a secret file that group or others can read or write: the TLS KeyFile and the ACME EABHMACKeyFile (since v0.6.0), as OpenSSH refuses a private key, with chmod 600 it. The mode is read from the opened file, not from its name. A replacement key written readable is not taken: the current certificate keeps serving and OnError is called. Not checked on Windows, where ACLs decide. Upgrade: chmod 600 (or 0400) both files before deploying.

What it is checked against

pebble, Let’s Encrypt’s test CA, run in-process from its ca, db, va and wfe packages with a DNS stub, issuing real certificates that crypto/tls verifies against pebble’s root: tls-alpn-01; http-01 through HTTPHandler and its control with HTTPChallenge off; EAB required, absent, wrong, then right;a pre-validated domain issued with no challenge port open, and its control. A test runs the same issuance without the golang/go#77704 workaround and requires it to fail. The coverage floor is 100%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/servercert@v0.7.0
